_about: Public-source EU-law demo course for the coverage map (pitch plan row 1). Everything here is written for the demo from public sources only (Treaty text on EUR-Lex, Court of Justice judgments, see docs/demo/eu-demo-sources-index.json). The 13 learning objectives are the ones written for the demo (docs/demo/eu-demo-learning-objectives.md): illustrative, not the objectives of any university course. The 9-week schedule is a demo schedule, not any course's week plan. No readers, slides, past exams or exam material were used. Cards are short statements of holdings from those judgments. The per-week authority chips are in blueprint.py (DEMO_AUTHORITIES).
sources: https://curia.europa.eu (Court of Justice judgments via the Publications Office Cellar)

course.name: EU Internal Market and Constitutional Foundations (demo)

brief.textbook: Public sources only: TFEU and Court of Justice judgments
brief.learning_objectives:
A1. State the prohibitions in Articles 34 and 35 TFEU and the derogation grounds in Article 36 TFEU. Explain the old numbering: Articles 30 to 36 EEC, then 28 to 30 EC, now 34 to 36 TFEU.
A2. Reproduce the Dassonville definition of an MEQR (Case 8/74, para 5) and explain why it is broad: "directly or indirectly, actually or potentially".
A3. Explain mutual recognition and the "mandatory requirements" in Cassis de Dijon (Case 120/78, paras 8 and 14). Distinguish them from the Article 36 TFEU grounds.
A4. Explain the Keck distinction between product requirements and certain selling arrangements (Joined Cases C-267/91 and C-268/91, paras 15 to 17). Apply its two conditions: the rules apply to all relevant traders; they affect domestic and imported products in the same manner, in law and in fact. The student can also explain precisely what Keck changed. Keck says "contrary to what has previously been decided" (para 16): it limits how the Dassonville formula applies to such selling arrangements. It does not abolish the formula.
A5. Set out the three-part summary in Commission v Italy (C-110/05, para 37), including the "market access" limb. Apply it to rules on how a product may be used (paras 56 to 58).
A6. Apply Keck to a modern sales channel, using Ker-Optika (C-108/09, paras 45 to 56). The national ban on internet sales of contact lenses is a selling arrangement. It fails the second Keck condition, so it is an MEQR.
A7. Assess a justification for appropriateness and necessity, using: road safety in Commission v Italy (paras 59 to 69, where the measure is justified); public health in Ker-Optika (paras 57 to 75, where the measure goes beyond what is necessary).
A8. Solve a problem question step by step: Is the measure an MEQR? Is it a product requirement or a selling arrangement, or a use restriction? Is there a justification? Is the measure proportionate? Cite the ECLI of each case relied on.
B1. Explain why Van Gend en Loos (Case 26/62) described the Community as "a new legal order of international law". State the conditions for a Treaty provision to have direct effect. The English text has no paragraph numbers, so the student cites it by ECLI and ECR page.
B2. Explain the reasoning in Costa v ENEL (Case 6/64): the Treaty created "its own legal system" that cannot "be overridden by domestic legal provisions, however framed". The text has no paragraph numbers.
B3. State the national court's duty in Simmenthal (Case 106/77, paras 21 and 24). In the words of para 24, a national court must "give full effect to those provisions, if necessary refusing of its own motion to apply any conflicting provision of national legislation, even if adopted subsequently", and it is "not necessary for the court to request or await the prior setting aside of such provision by legislative or other constitutional means".
B4. Explain why a directive "may not of itself impose obligations on an individual" (Marshall, Case 152/84, para 48). Explain why a directive can still be relied on against the State acting as employer (para 49).
B5. Describe the function of Article 267 TFEU and the effect of directives under Article 288 TFEU. Link each to the cases above.

cards.front: What do Articles 34 and 35 TFEU prohibit?
cards.back: Quantitative restrictions and measures having equivalent effect: on imports between Member States (Article 34) and on exports (Article 35). Article 36 TFEU lists the grounds on which they may be derogated from.

cards.front: How were Articles 34 to 36 TFEU numbered before the Lisbon Treaty?
cards.back: Articles 30 to 36 EEC, then Articles 28 to 30 EC, now Articles 34 to 36 TFEU.

cards.front: What is the Dassonville formula for a measure having equivalent effect (Case 8/74, para 5)?
cards.back: All trading rules enacted by Member States which are capable of hindering, directly or indirectly, actually or potentially, intra-Community trade.

cards.front: What did Cassis de Dijon (Case 120/78) add to the Dassonville formula?
cards.back: Mutual recognition (goods lawfully produced and marketed in one Member State may in principle enter another) and the "mandatory requirements" that can justify indistinctly applicable rules (para 8). They are distinct from the Article 36 TFEU grounds.

cards.front: Keck (C-267/91 and C-268/91): when do selling arrangements fall outside Article 34 TFEU?
cards.back: When the rules apply to all relevant traders and affect the marketing of domestic and imported products in the same manner, in law and in fact (paras 15 to 17).

cards.front: Did Keck abolish the Dassonville formula?
cards.back: No. Keck says "contrary to what has previously been decided" (para 16): it limits how the formula applies to certain selling arrangements. Product requirements remain MEQRs (para 15).

cards.front: What are the three limbs in Commission v Italy (C-110/05, para 37)?
cards.back: Discriminatory measures; product requirements; and any other measure which hinders access of products to the market of a Member State (the market access limb).

cards.front: Commission v Italy (trailers): was the rule on use of trailers justified?
cards.back: The use restriction hinders market access (paras 56 to 58), so it is an MEQR, but it was justified on road safety grounds as appropriate and necessary (paras 59 to 69).

cards.front: Ker-Optika (C-108/09): how did the Court classify the ban on internet sales of contact lenses?
cards.back: As a selling arrangement that fails the second Keck condition (it affects imported products more), so it is an MEQR (paras 45 to 56).

cards.front: Ker-Optika: why was the public-health justification not accepted?
cards.back: The ban went beyond what is necessary to protect public health (paras 57 to 75).

cards.front: What are the four steps of a goods problem question?
cards.back: 1. Is the measure an MEQR? 2. Is it a product requirement, a selling arrangement or a use restriction? 3. Is there a justification? 4. Is the measure proportionate? Cite the ECLI of each case relied on.

cards.front: Van Gend en Loos (Case 26/62): how did the Court describe the Community?
cards.back: As "a new legal order of international law" for whose benefit the States have limited their sovereign rights.

cards.front: Van Gend en Loos: why could the Treaty provision be relied on by an individual?
cards.back: It contained a clear and unconditional prohibition, a negative rather than a positive obligation, which Member States could not qualify by any reservation.

cards.front: Costa v ENEL (Case 6/64): what did the Treaty create?
cards.back: Its own legal system, which became an integral part of the legal systems of the Member States and cannot be overridden by domestic legal provisions, however framed.

cards.front: Simmenthal (Case 106/77, para 24): what must a national court do with conflicting national law?
cards.back: Give full effect to the Community provisions, if necessary refusing of its own motion to apply any conflicting national legislation, even if adopted subsequently, without waiting for its prior setting aside.

cards.front: Marshall (Case 152/84, para 48): can a directive impose obligations on an individual?
cards.back: No. A directive may not of itself impose obligations on an individual, so it has no horizontal direct effect.

cards.front: Marshall (para 49): against whom can a directive be relied on?
cards.back: Against the State, including when it acts as employer.
